subject: Policy Q&A: snapshot immutability during failover and subsequent deletion propagation
messages:
From: Alex Rios <alex.rios@fintechco.com>
To: Jasmine Liu <jasmine.liu@redwood.com>
Cc: LegalOps <legalops@fintechco.com>
Date: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 09:15:00 -0800
Subject: Question: behavior of backups after DR cutover and deletion propagation

Hi Jasmine —

Thanks for taking this. A couple of questions from our security/compliance and SRE folks about how Redwood handles backups and deletes when we do a DR failover/cutover:

1) If we perform a failover (restore snapshots into a DR region) and later delete the original snapshots in the primary region due to retention policies, will those deletes propagate and remove the DR copies as well? We need to understand whether deletion is per-copy or global.

2) Can we set an immutability/retention flag on the snapshots that prevents deletes for X days, and does that also apply to replicated copies? Our compliance team is asking for a 90-day immutability guarantee after cutover for legal reasons.

3) If a legal hold is applied to a specific dataset after cutover, how does that interact with backup garbage collection and cross-region replication? Will a tombstone in one region block deletion in the other?

4) What is the typical timeline for deletion propagation and tombstone reconciliation — minutes, hours, days? We operate under tight SLAs so this is important.

I've attached our internal requirements spreadsheet for context.

Appreciate any detail you can share, and if helpful we can hop on a short call next week.

Thanks,
Alex
Alex Rios
SRE Manager, FinTechCo
alex.rios@fintechco.com

From: Jasmine Liu <jasmine.liu@redwood.com>

Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.com>, Dylan Brooks <dylan.brooks@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Question: behavior of backups after DR cutover and deletion propagation

Hi Alex —

Thanks for the detailed questions and the spreadsheet — that's really helpful. Looping in Marissa from Platform Reliability and Karthik from Security so they can confirm specifics. Quick high-level answers below, then Marissa will follow up with an authoritative playbook.

High-level summary (short answers):
- Deletes are per-snapshot-copy by default; a delete request targets a specific replica unless configured otherwise.
- We support an "immutable snapshot" flag (WORM-like) which is honored across replication if enabled at creation time; it prevents user-initiated deletes for the configured retention window.
- Legal holds are sticky and can override routine GC, but they must be applied to the canonical object identifier and flagged across replicas so GC respects them.
- Propagation of tombstones and reconciliation typically completes within the delete-queue window (usually a few minutes to a couple of hours under normal load), but cross-region reconciliation can extend up to 24 hours in edge cases (network partitions, retries).

Questions for you to help us answer precisely:
- Do you create a new snapshot during failover (i.e., a fresh copy in the DR region), or are you relying on a replicated copy that becomes the primary?
- Is the 90-day immutability requirement retroactive (apply to already-created snapshots) or only moving forward from the point of cutover?

Next steps: Marissa will paste the formal section from our DR retention playbook into this thread and highlight recommended config knobs for FinTechCo's 90-day needs.

— Jasmine
Jasmine Liu
Customer Solutions, Redwood Inference

From: Alex Rios <alex.rios@fintechco.com>
To: Jasmine Liu <jasmine.liu@redwood.com>
Cc: LegalOps <legalops@fintechco.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.com>, Dylan Brooks <dylan.brooks@redwood.com>
Date: Mon, 23 Nov 2026 08:30:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Question: behavior of backups after DR cutover and deletion propagation

Thanks Jasmine — quick clarifications:

- During the failover we generally restore from snapshots and instantiate new volumes in the DR region; however we also expect replication to be enabled in our account so there may be replicated copies present. For compliance we need the guarantee that once the cutover occurs, the preserved snapshot copy (whether replicated or newly created) cannot be deleted for 90 days unless explicitly released by FinTechCo LegalOps.
- The 90-day immutability needs to apply retroactively to any snapshot that was used in the cutover. If a snapshot that is older than 90 days is part of the failover, LegalOps may still apply a hold to extend retention, but our ask is that Redwood provides a simple configuration or support process to mark affected snapshots immutable for 90 days from cutover time.

Thanks — attached was our internal mapping of datasets to compliance class.

Alex

From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
To: Alex Rios <alex.rios@fintechco.com>
Cc: Jasmine Liu <jasmine.liu@redwood.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.com>, Dylan Brooks <dylan.brooks@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Question: behavior of backups after DR cutover and deletion propagation

Hi Alex —

Appreciate the clarifications. Below is the definitive guidance from our DR/retention playbook tailored to the FinTechCo scenario, plus operational recommendations and known caveats.

1) Replication vs. new restore semantics
- If a snapshot is replicated to the DR region (replica of the canonical snapshot object), deletes operate on the replica id unless you request cascade-delete. By default Redwood will not issue cross-replica cascade deletes; deleting the source snapshot will not automatically scrub replicas unless a cross-region purge policy is invoked.
- When you perform a restore-and-create (new volumes from a snapshot in DR), those volumes are independent objects; deletion of the original snapshot does not remove volumes created from it.

2) Immutability / retention flag behavior
- We offer an immutable retention flag that can be applied at snapshot creation or retroactively via API if the snapshot is still present and not already tombstoned. When the immutable flag is set AND replication is enabled for that snapshot, Redwood will propagate the immutability attribute to replicated copies within the same retention system. This is designed to meet WORM-like requirements.
- For retroactive immutability after cutover, we recommend using our "hold-on-cutover" API call which: (a) creates a short-lived canonical hold, (b) pushes the immutability flag to replicas, and (c) records the cutover event in the audit log for legal traceability. We can also perform this as a support-assisted job if you prefer that route.

3) Legal hold interactions
- Legal holds override routine GC across replicas if the hold is applied to the canonical object identifier and replicated via our metadata replication channel. If a hold is applied only locally (e.g., to a DR copy without the canonical mapping), GC may still remove other copies. So for compliance, we strongly advise applying holds via the canonical API (we can provide a one-click script).

4) Tombstone and reconciliation timing
- Typical delete/tombstone propagation: 1–30 minutes under normal operating conditions.
- In cases of cross-region congestion or multi-day partitions, reconciliation may take up to 24 hours. We mark objects as tombstoned and then sweep; tombstones are visible in the audit log immediately.

Operational recommendations for FinTechCo (actionable):
- Enable replication for the snapshot policy used during your cutover windows.
- Use the "hold-on-cutover" API (we will provide a wrapper script) to retroactively mark any snapshot used in the failover as immutable for 90 days from the cutover timestamp. This will propagate the immutability flag to replicated copies.
- If LegalOps needs the ability to release holds, request an access control exception for the LegalOps principal; we recommend an approval flow (Doc link below).
- We will file a support runbook (SUP-4521) to automate marking and audit logging for your next planned DR exercise.

Caveats / gotchas:
- If a snapshot was previously tombstoned and GC completed in the source region before you apply retroactive immutability, we cannot resurrect a fully GC'd object — you must restore from retained copies or backups.
- Immutability propagation requires metadata replication; if replication was disabled for an older snapshot, propagation may not occur automatically. We can detect and remediate with a support job but per-snapshot intervention may be needed.

Attachments: I've attached our DR retention playbook excerpt for the relevant sections and a short runbook template. If you'd like, we can schedule a 30-minute run-through with our Platform Reliability team to walk through your spreadsheet and map specific snapshot IDs to actions.

Best,
Marissa Cole
Director, Platform Reliability — Redwood Inference
marissa.cole@redwood.com
